The Golden Girls Songwriter Made a Darkstalkers Theme

video // Nov 18, 2026 · Updated Nov 20, 2026

Watch on YouTube

In short

Eikichi Yazawa’s “The Trouble Man” connects Darkstalkers to Andrew Gold, the songwriter behind “Thank You for Being a Friend.” Gold wrote the English lyrics; Yazawa composed and performed the song. My documentary follows it from a 1995 Japanese CD single through PlayStation, television and anime, explains the missing soundtrack track, and revisits the memories and revival hopes that have kept it alive.

Watch the full XFD documentary on YouTube · Watch the Facebook companion reel

Before the song, there were the monsters

Watch from 0:51

Capcom’s 1994 fighting game was called Vampire in Japan and Darkstalkers: The Night Warriors overseas. Its cast gave familiar horror creatures their own fighting-game personalities: Morrigan the succubus, Demitri the vampire, a werewolf, a mummy, and Lord Raptor, a zombie rock guitarist.

The main series moved quickly through three games by 1997. What followed was a much longer wait for another main entry, even as reissues and collections brought the older games back. That history matters because the music remained familiar to people who encountered Darkstalkers in very different ways. You could know the song from a cartoon without ever owning the Japanese PlayStation game.

The answer is on a 1995 CD sleeve

Watch from 1:21

The singer is Eikichi Yazawa, the Japanese rock star fans call the Boss. The film introduces his career with Carol in the early 1970s, his move into solo work in 1975, and the scale of his following. His 150th Nippon Budokan performance came in 2023. That is the artist behind this fighting-game theme, rather than a singer hired for one isolated cartoon song. Yazawa’s official tour record

On May 24, 1995, Yazawa released “Aozora.” Its second track was “The Trouble Man.” The official discography credits Andrew Gold with the lyrics and Yazawa with the composition, under catalogue number TODT-3490. Official single listing and credits

In the documentary, I show the physical sleeve identifying the song as Capcom’s Vampire opening theme. That small piece of packaging is useful evidence: the game connection was there on the record itself. It was not something fans attached to the song years later.

Where The Golden Girls comes in

Watch from 2:23

Andrew Gold is the connection. He had “Lonely Boy” in 1977 and wrote “Thank You for Being a Friend,” released in 1978 and later used as the theme for The Golden Girls. In 1995, his English lyrics were coming out of Yazawa’s mouth on “The Trouble Man.” The title of this documentary is about that songwriting connection, not a claim that Gold sang the Darkstalkers recording.

The credits also make more sense once you look beyond the two television themes. Gold and Yazawa already had a substantial working history. Gold’s official guest discography lists production or co-production credits on eight Yazawa albums between 1984 and 1994: E., Yokohama, Tokyo Nights, Flash in Japan, Eikichi, I Don’t Wanna Stop, Heart, and The Name Is Yazawa. “The Trouble Man” grew out of an established musical relationship. Andrew Gold’s official guest discography

That is the part I love about following a credit. A song I remembered from Darkstalkers led to somebody I knew from somewhere completely different.

The Japanese PlayStation opening

Watch from 3:34

The Japanese PlayStation version of Vampire arrived in March 1996 with a CG opening. Demitri rises against the moon, and “The Trouble Man” gives the sequence its voice. The documentary also shows the song’s use in Japanese television advertising.

This is a specific version of the game, not an opening shared by every Darkstalkers release. The original arcade game did not have that PlayStation CG introduction. The film also identifies another Yazawa song, “The Rain,” with the PlayStation ending, though the opening is the sequence at the centre of this story.

The single’s 1995 release and the PlayStation game’s 1996 release are worth keeping separate. The dated sleeve gives us evidence of the song’s Vampire association before that home version reached shops.

Why you could buy the anime soundtrack and still miss the song

Watch from 4:10

The anime soundtrack is where the story gets frustrating for anyone trying to track the song down. The 1997 soundtrack shown in the film has 21 tracks, but “The Trouble Man” is not one of them. Its August 27 release date and track list are on the physical release used in the documentary.

That soundtrack contains Kow Otani’s score. The film draws on its liner notes to discuss the mix of hard rock, orchestral writing and avant-garde elements. The ending song is a separate part of the anime’s musical identity, and buying the score did not automatically get you that recording.

For years, the original single was the route discussed in the film. The song did not join Yazawa’s album catalogue until the 2022 non-album-tracks collection, アルバム未収録集, released as part of his 50th-anniversary digital remaster campaign. The official recording is available to hear now. Listen to the official “The Trouble Man” upload · Sony Music’s 2022 release announcement

That is a 27-year gap from the single to the collection. It does not mean the song was unreleased for 27 years. The CD existed, and the missing soundtrack listing alone does not tell us why the song was left off.

One song, several ways into Darkstalkers

Watch from 5:39

“The Trouble Man” also plays over the end credits of the 1995 American cartoon. Later, it closes all four episodes of Madhouse’s Darkstalkers anime. The documentary looks at those anime endings, including the character-painted guitars, alongside the game and television footage.

Those appearances explain why the song can trigger different memories. For one viewer it is the Japanese PlayStation opening. For another it is the cartoon’s credits. For somebody else it is the last thing they heard after an anime episode.

Fan uploads and conversations have helped people find it again. Calling it an anthem is a way of describing that attachment, not an official designation from Capcom. The song kept travelling even while fans waited for the games to move forward.

The bat emoji and the hope for another game

Watch from 6:53

The documentary brings that long wait into the story. Darkstalkers Resurrection revisited Night Warriors and Darkstalkers 3 in 2013. Capcom Fighting Collection included five Darkstalkers games in 2022, giving the series another way to reach players. Capcom’s collection announcement

Then there is the October 2024 post from Street Fighter 6 director Takayuki Nakayama. As covered in the film, he recalled an older fighting-game project that was not Street Fighter, added a bat emoji, and described development stopping and the team moving to mobile work. Fans naturally wondered about Darkstalkers. His follow-up complicated that reading rather than confirming the game people wanted.

The film also discusses Street Fighter 6’s Darkstalkers-themed pass and trademark filings in Europe and Japan. These are reasons the name keeps coming up, but a costume, a trademark or a suggestive emoji is not a new-game announcement. The documentary does not treat them as one.

If Darkstalkers does return, I would love to hear this song with it. That is a fan’s wish, not news about a soundtrack or a confirmed project.

Why I went looking for it

Watch from 8:09

My introduction was the cartoon on UPN in the fall of 1995. I remember Morrigan, a red moon and that song. I later got Darkstalkers 3, but the sound was already part of how I remembered the series.

Years later, finding footage on YouTube brought the memory back. The clip I rediscovered was a Japanese game commercial. Its moonlit imagery and music took me straight back to watching the cartoon. That is my recollection of encountering Darkstalkers, not proof that the same Japanese commercial aired during my UPN broadcast.

Following that memory took me to a CD sleeve, soundtrack credits, Yazawa’s catalogue and Andrew Gold. The documentary is the full trip, with the music and footage that made me want to investigate in the first place.

Where did you first hear “The Trouble Man”: the cartoon, PlayStation or the anime? Leave a comment on the video. If this was your first time hearing it, welcome to the night.
